title: Effect of caloric restriction on organ size and its contribution to metabolic adaptation: an ancillary analysis of CALERIE 2

sections.abstract: Caloric restriction (CR) can enhance human health, though underlying mechanisms, particularly related to energy expenditure, remain unclear. This ancillary investigation of the only randomized controlled trial of long-term CR in normal-weight adults, aimed to quantify metabolic adaptation following weight loss by assessing changes in energy-expending tissues and organs using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Participants in the CR group were prescribed 24-month 25% CR causing a ~ 13% weight loss at 12 months followed by 12 month weight maintenance, whereas the control group maintained ad libitum food intake throughout. The CR group experienced reductions in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle mass compared to the control group. Sleeping energy expenditure decreased more than predicted at 12 months, regardless of whether predictions were based on body mass, dual x-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-derived body composition, or MRI-derived tissue mass. MRI-derived models explained slightly more variation in energy expenditure at baseline and detected greater metabolic adaptation than simpler models based on body mass only. At 24 months, only the models based on DXA and MRI were indicative of persistent metabolic adaptation. These findings highlight the complexity of metabolic responses to CR. Further, advanced imaging techniques hold potential to provide insight into organ-specific contributions to energy metabolism during CR.
sections.introduction:
Caloric restriction (CR) extends lifespan and promotes healthspan in various organisms 1 . Preclinical studies have provided compelling evidence that supports various beneficial effects of prolonged reductions in caloric intake 1 , yet the translation of these findings into the clinical setting remains a topic of active investigation 2 , particularly because underlying mechanisms in the context of human physiology are unknown.

Weight loss induced by CR is comprised of losses to different bodily tissues, including adipose and fat-free tissues 3 – 5 and bone 6 , 7 . The proportion of loss that occurs in each tissue varies depending on multiple factors, including initial body mass, macronutrient composition of the diet, level of physical activity, biological sex, and others 8 – 10 . We and others have explored whether and to what degree CR affects the mass of different components of fat-free tissue 11 , 12 ; this includes the mass of the brain, kidneys, and the liver which are crucial to the maintenance of optimal bodily function. In the Comprehensive Assessment of Long-term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy (CALERIE) Phase 2 trial 13 , we observed that ~ 13% CR over 24 months led to a preferential loss of fat (78% of total tissue loss) over lean (17.5% of total tissue loss) tissue but with no difference in organ volume change compared to an ad libitum (AL) control group 12 . However, changes in liver volume as well as skeletal muscle and adipose tissue were related to the degree of CR 12 , whereas change in liver fat was not related to change in liver volume change as previously reported 12 . Changes in these bodily compartments are important to evaluate if CR is to be used therapeutically to extend healthspan and to uncover physiological mechanisms for human longevity.

For the body to control energy balance in the context of reduced nutrient availability, CR has been demonstrated to induce energy metabolism changes including a lowering of metabolic rate. In resting conditions, this reduced energy expenditure arises partly because of a lower thermic effect of food secondary to reduced energy intake and, when sustained, the body having a lower metabolic demand due to its reduced mass 14 . However, the reduction in energy expenditure that is observed in the context of CR often surpasses what is expected for the loss in body mass 15 , 16 . Similarly, the reduction in energy expenditure also remains only partially explained when the losses in fat mass and fat-free mass are independently considered 17 . However, fat-free mass constitutes many organs and tissues which have varying metabolic rates, with many organs having metabolic rates several fold times higher than skeletal muscle 18 , 19 . Hence, the CR-induced changes to metabolic rate could be further understood with measuring the changes in organ size and evaluating the contribution of organ size changes to energy metabolism. The purpose of this study was therefore to more precisely quantify CR-induced metabolic adaptation (MA), also termed adaptive thermogenesis, by considering changes to organ sizes measured by whole body MRI.
sections.methods:
This was an NIH-funded ancillary study conducted in a subset of participants enrolled in the CALERIE 2 ( NCT00427193 ) trial at Pennington Biomedical Research Center. CALERIE 2 was a multicenter randomized clinical trial that tested the efficacy of a 24-month intervention targeting a sustained 25% CR compared to a comparator group that ate AL 13 , 20 . The ancillary study protocol for this study was approved by the institutional review boards at Pennington Biomedical Research Center (Baton Rouge, LA) and Columbia University Irving Medical Center (New York, NY). All participants provided written, informed consent for study procedures prior to data collection, which was performed according to relevant guidelines and regulations.

Individuals in CALERIE 2 were healthy with a body mass index (BMI) between 22.0 to less than 28.0 kg/m 2 at enrollment. Males were aged between 21 and 50 years and females were aged between 21 and 47 years to minimize the effects of menopause onset during the trial. Participants were randomized with a 2:1 allocation to either the CR or AL group, with randomization stratified by sex and BMI. Details about the intervention have previously been reported 13 . Briefly, the CR intervention targeted an immediate and sustained 25% restriction of energy intake from baseline energy requirements as determined by doubly labeled water 24 , 25 for the first 12 months followed by 12 months of subsequent weight maintenance. A mathematical model predicting weekly changes in body mass was used to guide adherence to the intervention and CR participants followed an intensive behavioral intervention 26 , 27 . For the ancillary study analysis, we only included individuals that were “adherent” given their assigned treatment groups; that is, individuals that showed > 5% decrease in body mass at both follow-up time points if they were in the CR group, and individuals that showed < 5% change in body mass at both time points if they were in the AL group 28 . This criterion resulted in exclusion of two participants and a resulting sample size of 42 participants.

Demographics, anthropometric variables, measures of body composition using dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), and sleeping energy expenditure in a whole room indirect calorimeter were collected as part of the parent study.

Demographic variables including age and biological sex were collected at baseline. Height was measured in duplicate at baseline without shoes to the nearest 0.5 cm using a wall-mounted stadiometer. Body mass was measured in duplicate in the morning following an overnight fast at baseline, midpoint (12 months), and end (24 months) of the trial using an electric scale (Scale Tronix 5200; Welch Allyn) with participants wearing a hospital gown and no shoes. The weight of the gown was subtracted to obtain true metabolic body mass. BMI was calculated as body mass divided by meters squared.

Body composition (i.e., fat mass and fat-free mass) was assessed using DXA at baseline, 12 months, and 24 months (Hologic 4500A, Delphi W or Discovery A scanners). Scans were performed following standardized procedures for subject positioning and scan mode, and all scans were analyzed at a central reading center by blinded analysts.

At baseline, midpoint (month 12), and end (month 24) of the trial, whole-body MRI scans were acquired in the Biomedical Imaging Core at Pennington Biomedical using a 3.0 T Sigma Excite system (General Electric, Milwaukee, WI). MRI images were acquired from the tips of the fingers with arms stretched above the head to the bottom of the feet 29 , 30 . A 3D gradient echo sequence with a repetition time of 3.5 ms and an echo time of 1.7 ms was used for acquisition of the whole-body MRI scans using a torso phase array coil. The acquisition matrix was 380 by 192, and the slice thickness of the contiguous axial slice was 3.4 mm. For brain imaging, axial contiguous brain MRI scans were acquired using a spin echo sequence with a slice thickness of 5 mm, a repetition time of 3500 ms, and an echo time of 98 ms. Following acquisition, images were segmented for adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, brain, liver, kidneys, and residual lean tissues (i.e., bones, tendons, connective tissue, and the digestive tract) at the Image Analysis Core Laboratory of New York Obesity Nutrition Research Center by a blinded experienced MRI technician using the image analysis software SliceOmatic 5.0 (Tomovision Inc., Montreal, Canada) 31 . Tissue compartment volume was calculated as previously described 32 . The intraclass correlation coefficient for volume rendering of brain, liver, kidneys, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue for the same scan by the same analysts at the Image Analysis Core Laboratory of New York Obesity Nutrition Research Center is 0.95–0.99 29 , 33 , 34 . MRI volume estimates were converted to tissue mass by using the assumed density of 1.04 kg/L for skeletal muscle, liver, and kidneys; 1.03 kg/L for brain; and 0.92 kg/L for adipose tissue 29 , 35 , 36 . The images could not be segmented for heart because the MRI sequences were not cardiac gated so there was no clear separation between blood and cardiac muscle. To approximate heart mass, we used a previously published equation with trunk lean mass derived from DXA 23 , 37 : heart mass (kg) = 0.012 * trunk lean mass (kg) 1.0499 .

Energy expenditure was assessed in a whole room indirect calorimeter as previously described 25 . Participants stayed in the room for 23.25 h and were provided with three meals and one snack at scheduled intervals with the instruction to consume all their food within 30 min. Meals were tailored such that individuals met the caloric target that aligned with their treatment group assignment; that is, participants in the CR group were fed 25% calories less than their baseline energy requirements, whereas participants in the AL group were fed to maintain energy balance 28 . Sleeping energy expenditure was calculated from VO 2 and VCO 2 according to the Weir equation 38 between 2 and 5 am when motion detectors in the chamber were recording no activity. We specifically decided to use sleeping energy expenditure as a robust measure of resting energy expenditure given its repeatability of over 95% across repeated measures and precision with an estimated measurement error of only ~ 2% 39 .

We derived three different prediction equations for sleeping energy expenditure at baseline. Firstly, we used multiple linear regression with sex, age, and body mass. Secondly, we built a model using sex, age, and fat mass and fat-free mass derived from DXA 28 . Thirdly, we employed previously established 18 and validated 19 values for tissue-specific energy expenditure to predict sleeping energy expenditure from sex, age, and adipose tissue, skeletal muscle mass, brain mass, liver mass, kidney mass, heart mass and residual lean mass from MRI. For comparison, and because we did not have a measurement of all organs included in the previously validated equation (i.e., heart mass), we also developed our own model using MRI-measured skeletal muscle, adipose tissue mass, and the combined mass of organs and tissues available (i.e., brain, liver, kidney, spleen, and residual lean tissue), in addition to age and sex.

Predicted values for sleeping energy expenditure were generated from each linear regression equation developed at baseline (body mass, DXA and MRI) for month 12 (the midpoint) and month 24 (end of the trial) using the actual body mass and composition values at those time points. The differences in the measured and predicted energy expenditure values (termed “residuals”) while accounting for the baseline error were calculated as a measure of metabolic adaptation (also termed adaptive thermogenesis); i.e., a change in energy expenditure that was not explained by the observed changes in tissue mass.

The primary outcome of this analysis was to more precisely quantify MA by considering changes in organ sizes as assessed via MRI in comparison to simpler models including either fat mass and fat-free mass derived from DXA, or body mass alone. All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.3.2). Baseline participant characteristics are presented as means (standard deviation) or N (percent) for continuous or categorical variables, respectively. Changes in outcome variables from baseline were analyzed using a linear mixed model with fixed effects for time and treatment group, the interaction thereof, and a random effect for participant to account for repeated measures. Within- and between-group effect estimates alongside corresponding 95% confidence intervals as derived from the model are reported for these analyses. Residuals (i.e., the difference between measured and predicted energy expenditure values) were derived from the different prediction equations while accounting for the error at baseline. These residual values were compared against zero to determine if statistically significant metabolic adaptation occurred. This was done with linear mixed models with fixed effects for the method of prediction and time as well as the interaction thereof, and a random effect for participant. Additionally, the different prediction methods were modeled as a continuous variable representing the increase in granularity of tissue assessment, and the interaction between this slope and the treatment group were assessed using a linear mixed model. Furthermore, individuals were classified categorically as having metabolic adaptation (or not) if the residual (i.e., the unexplained decrease in SleepEE) was greater than the measurement error of SleepEE, estimated at 2% 39 . Finally, the magnitude of metabolic adaptation was calculated as a percentage of SleepEE at each respective time point.

Participants in the CR group lost an average of 9.7 ± 2.2 kg ( P < 0.001) and 8.9 ± 2.4 kg ( P < 0.001) after 12 and 24 months, respectively. In contrast, the AL group experienced a slight increase in body mass of 1.3 ± 1.8 kg ( P = 0.02) and 2.7 ± 2.4 kg ( P < 0.001) at the two time points, respectively. This equated to a change of − 13.4 ± 3.1% and − 12.3 ± 3.5% from baseline body mass at the two time points in the CR group, compared to a change of 1.7 ± 2.4% and 3.9 ± 3.7% in the AL group. There were within-group decreases in the CR group in the mass of all tissues and organs assessed with MRI except for the kidneys. In contrast, there were no changes of any organs or tissues in the AL group except for adipose tissue that was increased at both follow-up time points, and residual lean mass that was increased at the end of the trial. Estimated heart mass decreased in the CR group compared to an increase in the AL group. As a result, there were statistically significant between-group changes over time for adipose tissue ( P < 0.001), skeletal muscle mass ( P < 0.001), and estimated heart mass ( P < 0.001) at both time points, as well as for residual lean mass at the end of the trial ( P < 0.01).

At baseline, sleeping energy expenditure (SleepEE) was comparable between the CR group (1523 ± 207 kcal/d) and the AL group (1512 ± 235 kcal/d). The equations to predict SleepEE from body mass (SleepEE BM ), DXA-derived body composition (SleepEE DXA ), and MRI-derived organ and tissue mass (SleepEE MRI ) at baseline were as follows. We built two prediction models using either previously established tissue-specific energy expenditure values (SleepEE MRI-ELIA ) or a regression model based on our data (SleepEE MRI-REGRESSION ). Despite the inclusion of different bodily compartments (i.e., different components of lean tissue), all models explained a similar proportion of variance of SleepEE at baseline, except that SleepEE MRI-REGRESSION model explained 4–6% more variance that the other models.

Measured SleepEE was not significantly changed in participants in the AL group at either the 12-month (2 kcal/d, 95% CI − 50 to 55 kcal/d, P = 0.93) or 24-month (− 13 kcal/d, 95% CI − 65 to 39 kcal/d, P = 0.62) time points compared to baseline. In contrast, SleepEE was significantly reduced in the CR group at both 12 (− 159 kcal/d, 95% CI − 198 to − 120 kcal/d, P < 0.001) and 24 months (− 137 kcal/d, 95% CI − 176 to − 98 kcal/d, P < 0.001). Correspondingly, there were significant differences in SleepEE change between groups at 12 months (− 162 kcal/d, 95% CI − 227 to − 96 kcal/d, P < 0.001) and 24 months (− 124 kcal/d, − 189 to − 58 kcal/d, P < 0.001).

To determine if there was a metabolic adaptation (adaptive thermogenesis) in response to the caloric restriction intervention (i.e., a larger reduction in SleepEE beyond what is explained by changes in tissue mass), we compared the measured change in SleepEE at each time point with the SleepEE change predicted from our prediction equations developed at baseline (Table 3 ). Regardless of the prediction equation (i.e., including body mass, DXA-derived body composition, or MRI-derived mass of organs and tissues), SleepEE was significantly lower than predicted (P < 0.05) at the 12-month time point, indicative of metabolic adaptation. In contrast, there was no evidence of lower-than-expected energy expenditure at 24 months as predicted using body mass only ( P = 0.14), whereas the models using DXA-derived body composition and MRI-derived organ and tissue mass resulted in statistically significant residuals, suggestive of greater than expected decrease in energy expenditure as metabolic adaptation (all P < 0.05) (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Metabolic adaptation (measured compared to predicted change in sleeping energy expenditure) based on changes in body mass (BM), DXA-derived body composition (DXA), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived organ and tissue mass based on a regression approach (MRI-REGR), or MRI-derived organ and tissue mass based on previously established coefficients (MRI-ELIA) after 12 or 24 months of a calorie restriction intervention (left) or ad libitum food intake (right). Data presented as means with standard deviation. Statistical significance of metabolic adaptation compared against 0 denoted via symbols; # , P < 0.05; $ , P < 0.01; *, P < 0.001.

Metabolic adaptation (measured compared to predicted change in sleeping energy expenditure) based on changes in body mass (BM), DXA-derived body composition (DXA), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived organ and tissue mass based on a regression approach (MRI-REGR), or MRI-derived organ and tissue mass based on previously established coefficients (MRI-ELIA) after 12 or 24 months of a calorie restriction intervention (left) or ad libitum food intake (right). Data presented as means with standard deviation. Statistical significance of metabolic adaptation compared against 0 denoted via symbols; # , P < 0.05; $ , P < 0.01; *, P < 0.001.

There was no statistically significant difference in the metabolic adaptation derived from the different prediction equations at any time point, except at month 12 where metabolic adaptation calculated from the equation using body mass only was smaller compared to when it was calculated from the equation regressed using MRI-derived skeletal muscle mass, fat mass, and organ mass (− 47, 95% CI − 90; − 3, P = 0.03). As expected, there was no evidence of metabolic adaptation in the control group (all P > 0.10). Additionally, there were no statistically significant differences between the metabolic adaptation values between the treatment groups (i.e., AL vs CR) within each prediction method used—that is, there was no statistically significant difference between AL and CR in the metabolic adaptation assessed with the prediction equation using body mass at 12 (32 kcal/d, 95% CI − 39 kcal/d; 102 kcal/d, P = 0.38) or 24 months (− 14 kcal/d, 95% CI − 84 kcal/d; 57 kcal/d, P = 0.70) and analogously for the other prediction equations. However, when the increase in granularity across the prediction methods (i.e., only body mass compared to organ and tissue mass) was modeled as a continuous slope, a significant interaction was apparent between this slope and the treatment group (28 kcal/d, 95% CI 18 kcal/d; 39 kcal/d, P < 0.001), suggestive of increasingly greater metabolic adaptation observed with greater precision of tissue assessment in the CR group compared to the AL group. sections.discussion:
In this ancillary investigation of the CALERIE 2 randomized clinical trial, participants underwent MRI assessments to examine tissue and organ mass at baseline, 12 months, and 24 months. The CR group exhibited substantial reductions in body mass with an average loss of ~ 13% from baseline after 12 and 24 months. In contrast, the AL group showed a small increase in body mass over the same period. MRI assessment demonstrated significant decreases in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle mass in the CR group compared to the AL group at both 12 and 24 months, a decrease in residual lean tissue mass at 24 months, and a near significant reduction ( P = 0.07) in liver mass at 12 months, consistent with what has been reported previously 12 .

The prediction equations developed at baseline and used to predict subsequent changes in energy expenditure based on change in bodily tissues explained between 70% (for equations based off prior literature) and 76% (for the equation including MRI-assessed organ and tissue mass) of energy expenditure variance at baseline. Mirroring the change in body mass, sleeping energy expenditure (the most reproducible measure of energy expenditure in resting condition) decreased in the CR group at 12 months to a greater extent than predicted by linear models based on either body mass alone, DXA-derived body composition, or MRI-derived tissue and organ sizes. Such results suggest the presence of metabolic adaptation in response to caloric restriction at 12 months. At 24 months in the CR group, there was no evidence of lower-than-expected energy expenditure when predicted using body mass only, whereas the models using DXA body composition or MRI-derived tissue and organ sizes resulted in detection of metabolic adaptation. These observations suggest the possibility that advanced body composition methods might be able to capture metabolic adaptation in cases where relying on a body weight scale alone would not. Although metabolic adaptation was detected by models using only body mass at month 12, models with MRI-derived tissue and organ mass detected higher metabolic adaptation than body mass, suggesting that measuring lean tissue composition (i.e., organ mass) might be important in quantifying metabolic adaptation. In contrast, there were no statistically significant differences between any other methods. In this regard it is of interest that the equation based off established tissue-specific metabolic rates (MRI Elia ) provided a similar fit and comparable estimates of metabolic adaptation. The tissues assessed via MRI in this study are particularly metabolically active organs (i.e., the liver, brain, and kidneys), and basing the energy expenditure prediction off these tissues explained 4–6% more variance in SleepEE at baseline compared to the equations using body mass only, or DXA-assessed fat mass and fat-free mass. However, despite the modestly improved predictive ability at baseline, accounting for the changes in MRI-assessed tissues in evaluating the unexplained changed in energy expenditure following caloric restriction (MRI Rregression ) did not further enhance understanding of the physiological underpinnings underlying metabolic adaptation as the observed degree thereof was comparable to the simpler model including DXA-assessed tissues. This could be in parts due to our relatively homogenous sample of participants with limited variability in organ and tissue size in our normal-weight participants, and/or to extraneous influences that were not assessed in study measures but might have affected energy expenditure differentially and added uncontrolled variability (e.g., behavioral factors in addition to physiological responses). These findings stand in contrast to previous studies that have assessed energy expenditure changes using MRI and found lower or non-significant values for metabolic adaptation 21 , 22 . It is unclear as to why the model with organ size included did not further explain more of the variance in energy expenditure changes in our study. Together, these data suggest the presence of metabolic adaptation that goes beyond what can be explained by changes in not only body mass in general but also highly metabolically active organ and tissue mass with distinct metabolic rates specifically 18 , 19 . Nonetheless, the energy expenditure coefficients that are available in the literature are old and mostly derived from in vitro or animal studies – as such, reevaluating the specific metabolic rates of various bodily tissues, including in the context of an intervention such as CR, would be of interest to provide further insight into the body’s attempt at maintaining energy homeostasis.

Limitations of this study include the somewhat small sample size as well as the specific population of study participants that included middle-aged adults at healthy body mass when enrolling in the study 13 , which may limit the generalizability of these findings. Future studies with larger and more diverse study populations would be of interest to confirm the herein presented findings and to explore changes in organ size and tissue mass as well as their association with changes in energy expenditure in the context of caloric restriction in study populations that may have the potential for greater benefit or higher risk of harm in response to caloric restriction (e.g., individuals with obesity or metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease). Furthermore, more advanced imaging technology could be explored to refine the assessment of individual organs and tissues. Unfortunately, we were unable to directly evaluate heart mass in the present study. Instead, we attempted to approximate the mass of this organ using a previously published equation that uses the trunk lean mass derived from DXA imaging 23 . Although the baseline values of heart mass for our study participants directly align with previously published data in very similar study populations 19 , it is likely that the observed changes in estimated heart mass do not directly reflect the actual changes observed in heart mass but rather are an artefact of our estimation method (i.e., trunk lean mass). Therefore, these values need to be interpreted with caution and should be confirmed in future studies with appropriate assessment methods such as cardiac gated MRI.

In conclusion, the findings presented in this study add to the evidence demonstrating profound effects of caloric restriction on body mass and composition as well as its metabolic consequences reflected in changes in energy expenditure. Furthermore, the data highlight the utility of imaging technology such as DXA or MRI in assessing changes in specific bodily organs and tissues that provide insight into the physiological adaptations associated with long-term caloric restriction.
